catalog_quote: Unlike Malay, PT exhibits word stress. In this dissertation, word stress will not be marked since it is non-phonemic and predictably falls on the final syllable. Like other Kerinci varieties, the final syllable of both underived and derived words is stressed (Steinhauer and Usman 1978). In the words of Steinhauer (2002: 4): Kerinci today has a clearly observable word stress and consequently phrase stress, namely on the final word syllable and on the final syllable of the phrase. Three strands of evidence support the historical validity of this observation. First, a greater variety of vowels is permitted in final syllables. Given that stressed syllables allow for more contrast than non-stressed syllables, final syllables in PT prove to be more prominent than initial syllables. Second, the schwa /ə/ – which characteristically only occurs in unstressed syllables – is not attested in word-final syllables. Third, word-final stress is clearly observable when PT speakers speak other languages. Hence, Kerinci speakers can easily be ‘detected’ when they speak Malay because of this tendency.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the last syllable of every word, simple or derived; the phrase likewise carries its main stress on its final syllable (final word), so a word's final-syllable stress is strongest phrase-finally and weaker phrase-medially. The same rule is stated first-hand for the Sungai Penuh dialect by Steinhauer & Usman 1978: 483 ('Word-stress in SP is non-phonemic: it falls always on the final syllable of a word', saved file) and Steinhauer 2002: 153 (saved file).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described. Dutch summary (p. 350) frames the system as a heavy accent on the last syllable of the phrase and a secondary accent on the last syllable of each word; Steinhauer 2002: 154 adds that compounds are intonationally one word with stress on the final syllable, whereas both halves of a reduplication keep practically the same stress pattern; Steinhauer & Usman 1978: 496 note equal stress on both parts of ABS-initial verb sequences vs predominant second-component stress in OBL-initial ones.
new_statements.exceptions: None to the final-stress rule. Schwa, said to occur only in unstressed syllables, is absent from word-final syllables except in the function word ŋə 'REL; and; with' (fn. 35). Ernanda notes Kerinci speakers' final stress is audible when they speak Malay/Indonesian.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (final syllable of every word) with a phrase level on top (final syllable of the phrase = final word bears main stress). Source is a dissertation on the Pondok Tinggi dialect; Sungai Penuh is covered first-hand by Steinhauer & Usman 1978 and Steinhauer 2002. Impressionistic description; no instrumental data. Prosody interacts with the ABS/OBL (phrase-final vs phrase-medial) word-shape alternation, which Steinhauer derives historically from final stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Ernanda 2017 describes the Pondok Tinggi dialect (a satellite village of Sungai Penuh, Kerinci regency, Jambi); Steinhauer & Usman 1978 and Steinhauer 2002 describe the Sungai Penuh dialect, the main dialect of Kerinci (keri1250). Both are dialects of the same Glottolog language; the Glottolog languoid JSON lists no dialect children, so no dialect glottocodes are given. All three sources agree on non-phonemic final word stress, and Ernanda states it holds for 'other Kerinci varieties' too.

sources.note: §2.1 (i), p. 153 (PDF p. 5): 'Sungai Penuh Kerinci today has a clearly observable word stress and consequently phrase stress, namely on the final word syllable and on the final syllable of the phrase.' Phrase-final word bears main phrase/sentence stress with a rise-fall on its final syllable (pp. 153-154); compounds are intonationally one word with stress on the final syllable, reduplications keep near-equal stress on both parts (p. 154). Argues the ABS/OBL word-shape alternation arose historically from this final-stress intonation.
